pairs.en: **Matthew 19:16.**
*"And, behold, one came and said to Him, Good Master, by doing what shall I inherit eternal life?"* [Matthew 19:16]

Some accuse this young man of dissembling and ill will, of coming to Christ as if to test him. But I would not go so far as to call him a dissembler — both because it is unsafe to venture blame on an uncertain matter, and because Mark removes the suspicion himself: he tells us that the man came running to Jesus, knelt before him, and that *"Jesus, beholding him, loved him."* [Mark 10:17-21] Yet great is the tyranny of wealth — even a man virtuous in every other respect can be ruined by it alone; rightly does Paul call the love of money *the root of all evils.*

sections.heading: Why do you call me good?

pairs.en: Why then does Christ answer him, *"Why callest thou me good? There is none good but one, that is, God"*? Not putting himself outside of goodness — far from it — but speaking to the young man as a mere man might, a Jewish teacher, since that is all this man, at this point, took him to be. *There is none good* means: none among mere men, in comparison with the goodness of God; Christ added *but one — that is, God* rather than *my Father*, so that his listener might not yet learn that Christ himself had a claim to that goodness he had not revealed. Christ leads the young man on little by little, weaning him from flattery, and turning him toward God and the things to come.

And note how far along this man already was in willingness: not tempting Christ, but earnestly asking, *By doing what shall I inherit eternal life?* — so ready for obedience that when told to keep the commandments, he asked, *Which?* And when told these, he said, *All these have I kept from my youth up: what lack I yet?* Had he come tempting Christ, the evangelist would have told us so, as he does elsewhere; and had he come with an evil will, he would not have gone away *sorrowful* at what he heard — this alone shows a will too weak, not a will that was wicked.

sections.heading: Sell what you have, and come, follow me

pairs.en: **Matthew 19:21.**
*"If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me."* [Matthew 19:21]

See how many prizes, how many crowns Christ sets before this contest. Had he been testing the man with a trap, he would not have shown him such a reward. Instead, before even naming the toil, Christ names the prize: *If thou wilt be perfect* — then only after that, *sell that thou hast and give to the poor* — and then the reward again, *treasure in heaven,* and *come, follow me*, for to follow Christ is itself a great recompense. Christ gives the young man far more than he asks him to give up — as much more as heaven exceeds earth, and more even than that. It is not enough merely to despise wealth; we must also feed the poor, and above all, follow Christ — that is, do all that he commands, ready even for death, for *"if any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me."* [Matthew 16:24] To give away money is a far smaller thing than that last command, to give one's very blood — yet being freed from wealth contributes greatly toward it.

sections.heading: He went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions

pairs.en: **Matthew 19:22.**
*"But when the young man heard that saying, he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions."* [Matthew 19:22]

The evangelist adds this cause — *for he had great possessions* — to show that his grief was no accident: those who have little are not held so tightly in wealth's grip as those overflowing with abundance, for possession only inflames the passion further. See what power this passion showed even here: the man who had come to Christ with joy and eagerness, once told to cast away his riches, could not even bring himself to answer, but went away weighed down, dejected, and silent.

sections.heading: Easier for a camel than a rich man

pairs.en: *"Then said Jesus unto his disciples, Verily I say unto you, That a rich man shall hardly enter into the kingdom of heaven. And again I say unto you, It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God."* [Matthew 19:23-24]

Christ does not blame riches themselves, but those who are enslaved by them — for if the rich man enters only with difficulty, how much more the covetous man, who takes what belongs to others as well as clinging to his own! And why does Christ say this to his disciples, who were poor men owning nothing? To keep them from being ashamed of their poverty, as if excusing himself to them for having let them have nothing. Having first said it was *hard*, Christ then shows it is, in the highest degree, *impossible* — using the image of the camel and the needle's eye, so that his hearers might see that only the greatest grace could accomplish such a thing.

sections.heading: With God all things are possible

pairs.en: *"When his disciples heard it, they were exceedingly amazed, saying, Who then can be saved? But Jesus beheld them, and said unto them, With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible."* [Matthew 19:25-26]

Why should the disciples, being poor and owning nothing, be so troubled by this saying? Because of their tender care for the salvation of the whole world — they had already taken up, in their hearts, the compassion proper to teachers, and so trembled and feared on behalf of everyone else. Christ first looks on them gently, calming their shuddering minds, and only then speaks his word of comfort, setting before them the power of God.

And this saying is not meant to make us give up as if the thing were simply impossible, but to make us consider the greatness of the good work still to be attained, and to hasten toward it, praying for God's help in so noble a contest. How, then, does the impossible become possible? By casting away what we have, by emptying ourselves of excess wealth, by cutting off the greed within. Christ himself shows this is not left to God's power alone but requires our own effort, for immediately after, when Peter says, *"Behold, we have forsaken all, and followed thee; what shall we have therefore?"* Christ answers by naming the reward: *"every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren... shall receive an hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life."* [Matthew 19:27-29] So the impossible becomes possible — not all at once, but little by little, as one climbs a ladder step by step toward heaven.

sections.heading: The lust for wealth is never satisfied by more

pairs.en: Just as those suffering from an acrid bile in fever only inflame their thirst the more they eat and drink, so the covetous man, pouring more wealth onto his desire, does not quench it but sets it further ablaze. Nothing so restrains this sickness as abstaining, for a time, from the pursuit of gain — as bile is restrained by fasting rather than by feeding. Consider: who suffers more torment — the man who longs for costly food he cannot have, or the man who has no such longing at all? Clearly the one who desires and cannot obtain. This is exactly the torment Christ describes in the rich man of the parable, tormented for a single drop of water he could not have. [Luke 16:19-31] The man who despises wealth quiets his own desire; the man who craves it only inflames it further — for even with ten thousand talents he will want twice as much, and having that, twice again, until he desires the mountains, the sea, and the whole earth turned to gold for him, mad with a hunger that can never be put out by addition, only by taking away.

Consider: if you longed, absurdly, to fly through the air, how would you cure yourself of that desire — by building wings, or by persuading your own mind that the thing is simply impossible and ought not to be attempted at all? Clearly, by persuading the mind. So it is with the love of money: it is easier for a man to fly than to satisfy this lust by adding more to it. When a desire can actually be fulfilled, its owner may find peace in getting what he wants; but when it cannot, in principle, ever be satisfied, the only remedy is to draw the soul away from the desire itself.

sections.heading: The love of money as the root of every evil

pairs.en: Let us then put away this wicked desire for wealth. It is not even true that it gives us what is good in the present while only costing us the world to come — for even in this life it drags a man down into great misery, breaking apart households, stirring up wars, driving men to violent deaths, and before any of that, ruining the nobility of the soul, making the man who is enslaved to it cowardly, false, grasping, and given over to every worst thing.

If you are dazzled by the gleam of silver, the crowd of servants, the splendor of great houses, ask yourself instead how these things darken and disfigure the soul that owns them, with how many toils they were gained, with how much danger kept, and how death, in the end, will strip a man of all of it and leave him with nothing to carry away but the wounds his soul received in acquiring it. Consider Paul, consider Peter, consider John, consider Elijah — or rather the Son of God himself, who *"had not where to lay his head."* [Matthew 8:20] Be an imitator of him and of his servants, and reckon their unspeakable riches as your own true wealth.

The blessed Paul rightly called the love of money the *root of all evils* — for it is not the storing up of gold itself that condemns a man (gold, at least, is useful for other purposes, however small), but the burying and hoarding of it that serves no one, and kindles, for the man who misuses it, furnace after furnace of evil.

Let us then, considering all these things, set our hearts on what truly deserves emulation — not splendid buildings and costly estates, but the men who have great confidence toward God, who possess riches in heaven, who are truly rich because they have made themselves poor for Christ's sake — that we may attain to the good things of eternity, by the grace and love toward mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory, might, and honor, now and always, and unto ages of ages. Amen.
